term: Charles IX and Catherine de’ Medici
text: The French king Charles IX and his mother Catherine de’ Medici were blamed for the Saint Bartholomew’s Day Massacre of 1572, when thousands of Protestants were killed in Paris. Albert jokingly casts himself as an actor who has just played a part.
quote: Charles IX. put to Catherine de’ Medici

text: A long-stemmed Turkish tobacco pipe. Latakia is a fine, smoky tobacco from Syria.
quote: two chibouques filled with excellent latakia

text: A Balkan folk instrument, usually with a single string played with a bow.
quote: Haydée’s guzla

text: In Byron’s comic epic Don Juan (1819–24), Haidée is a beautiful Greek island girl who rescues the shipwrecked hero. Readers of the day knew the name from the poem.
quote: anywhere but in Byron’s poems

text: Dionysius II, tyrant of Syracuse, was driven from power in the 4th century BC and is said to have ended his days running a school in Corinth. People cited him as the classic example of fortune’s reversals.
quote: How was it that Dionysius the Tyrant became a schoolmaster?

text: Modern spoken Greek, as opposed to ancient Greek.
quote: asked the young girl in Romaic

text: Ioannina, a city in Epirus in northwest Greece, then part of the Ottoman Empire. Ali Pasha ruled from its fortress beside the lake, below the Pindus mountains.
quote: We were in the palace of Yanina

text: Pallikars: Greek and Albanian irregular soldiers famed for their courage. The word came to mean ‘brave young men’.
quote: the sashes of our Palikares

text: An Ottoman commander-in-chief. Hurshid (‘Kourchid’) Pasha led the sultan’s army against Ali Pasha in 1820–22.
A formal decree issued by the Ottoman sultan. ‘The master’ and ‘the emperor’ in Haydée’s story both mean the sultan.
quote: today arrives the firman of the master

text: Walter Scott’s 1819 novel, made into Donizetti’s popular 1835 opera. Edgar of Ravenswood bursts in just after his beloved has been made to sign a contract to marry another man.
quote: like the Laird of Ravenswood

text: An income of 300,000 francs a year is immense wealth: a skilled worker might earn around 1,000 francs a year. ‘Livre’ was the old name for the franc and was still used for sums and incomes.
quote: an income of 300,000 livres

text: A senior general’s rank, just below marshal in the French army. Morcerf puts on his uniform and all his decorations (‘crosses’) to make his proposal formal.
quote: his uniform of lieutenant-general

text: A real pistol gallery near the Champs-Élysées where Parisian gentlemen kept their aim sharp. The Allée des Veuves (now the Avenue Montaigne) was then a quiet, shady lane.
quote: Gosset’s shooting-gallery

text: In a duel each man named seconds, also called witnesses. They delivered the challenge, tried to arrange an apology, and if that failed they settled the place, the weapons and the rules.
quote: To be my second.

text: A public withdrawal of a printed statement. Under the code of honour, a man who felt insulted in print could demand one, and could challenge the writer if he refused.
quote: an entire retractation

text: Albert’s father sits in the Chamber of Peers, the upper house of the French parliament. Beauchamp is mocking Albert’s lordly tone.
quote: you are not in the Chamber

text: The Greeks rose against Ottoman rule in 1821, and the war ended with an independent Greek kingdom in 1832. Ali Pasha, who was himself in revolt against the sultan, fell in 1822, which is why the count says ‘1822 or 1823’.
quote: he fought for the independence of the Greeks

text: Under French law a person came of age at twenty-one. Until then a daughter needed her father’s consent to marry or to live under someone else’s roof.
quote: I shall wait till I am of age

text: After a close relative died, families wore black for many months. Valentine is in mourning for her grandparents.
quote: her deep mourning dress

text: A stroke, and the period’s catch-all word for any sudden collapse. The standard treatment was to bleed the patient by opening a vein.
quote: this is a fit of apoplexy

text: An antimony compound given to make a patient vomit. Ether and oil of turpentine were also used as stimulants and supposed antidotes.
quote: oil of turpentine and tartar emetic

text: A syrup made from violet petals. Like litmus paper, it changes colour when it meets certain substances, so it served as a simple chemical test.
quote: it turns syrup of violets green

text: Locusta was a notorious professional poisoner in 1st-century Rome. Agrippina, Nero’s mother, is said to have used her to poison the emperor Claudius.
quote: Locusta and Agrippina, living at the same time

text: Rival Frankish queens of the 6th century whose long feud was carried on through murders and assassinations.
quote: Brunhilda and Fredegund

term: Seek whom the crime will profit
text: The old legal maxim ‘is fecit cui prodest’, Latin for ‘he did it who profits by it’. It is the first rule of detection: look for whoever gains.
quote: Seek whom the crime will profit

text: In Hamlet the old courtier Polonius is stabbed through a curtain by Hamlet, who takes him for the king. He dies in someone else’s place.
quote: like Shakespeare’s Polonius, he died for another

text: A bitter poison closely related to strychnine and taken from the same plant. Doctors prescribed tiny doses for paralysis, but larger ones kill.
quote: I have given M. Noirtier brucine

text: A death sentence. In France criminals were executed in public by guillotine.
quote: To the scaffold with the poisoner

text: A huge sum, when a modest family might live on 2,000–3,000 francs a year. A dowry was the money a bride brought to her marriage, and the husband managed it.
quote: giving my daughter 500,000 francs as her dowry

text: The uniform worn by a household’s male servants. Dressed in his servant’s livery, Andrea passes unnoticed in the streets.
quote: You had a new livery yesterday?

text: The stock picture of a small Parisian shopkeeper living comfortably on an annuity in retirement. It is the modest respectability Caderousse claims to want.
quote: A retired baker?

text: A working-class district of eastern Paris. Picpus and the Rue Ménilmontant lay on the city’s poor eastern edge, far from Andrea’s fashionable haunts.
quote: walked down the Faubourg Saint-Antoine

text: French: ‘the host’s table’. A set meal served at fixed hours to all the guests of a hotel.
quote: the table d’hôte of the Hôtel des Princes

text: A luxurious restaurant on the Boulevard des Italiens, the most fashionable place to dine in Paris.
quote: or the Café de Paris

text: A later addition to a will that adds to it or changes it.
quote: are wills ever made without codicils?

text: Slang for gold coins. A louis was a 20-franc gold piece, so twenty-five louis make 500 francs. Caderousse wants silver five-franc pieces instead, because a poor man paying in gold attracts suspicion.
quote: Yellow boys?

text: A real firm of Paris locksmiths, famous for burglar-proof locks and safes.
quote: one of Huret & Fichet’s locks

text: Le Tréport, a fishing port on the Channel coast of Normandy, about 160 km north of Paris.
quote: go in one night from Paris to Tréport

text: A French league was about 4 km (2.5 miles). Fifty leagues in ten hours is astonishingly fast for travel by horse.
quote: fifty leagues in ten hours

text: In Schiller’s play Fiesco (1783), set in Genoa, the conspirator Fiesco catches the Moor hired to kill him and then takes him into his own service.
quote: over the Moor who would have killed him

text: A police magistrate in charge of a district, roughly a local police chief.
quote: the commissary of police

text: The Hôtel des Invalides, Louis XIV’s great hospital for old soldiers. Its clock could be heard across western Paris.
quote: The clock of the Invalides struck

text: Thieves’ slang for skeleton keys.
quote: which thieves call nightingales

text: Louis XVI was said to wear a mail vest for fear of assassins. He was guillotined in 1793, so the hatchet is the narrator’s figure of speech.
quote: was worn by King Louis XVI.

text: The square in front of the Paris Hôtel de Ville, where public executions took place for centuries.
quote: to the Place de Grève

text: Convicts were still said to go ‘to the galleys’. By now this meant the bagne, a forced-labour prison at naval ports such as Toulon, where chained convicts worked the docks and were known by numbers.
quote: I was only condemned to the galleys

text: A peninsula across the harbour from Toulon where convict gangs worked. Hyères is a coastal town a few miles to the east.
quote: We were working at Saint-Mandrier, near Toulon

text: A signed written statement to be used as evidence.
quote: Shall I write your deposition?

text: Murder was a capital crime in France, and the guillotine had been the means of execution since 1792.
quote: And he will be guillotined, will he not?

text: Caderousse’s crime could have cost him his head, but he got hard labour for life in the convict prison instead. A convicted felon lost his civil standing for good.
quote: to transport me for life, how merciful!

text: The Paris Morgue, near Notre-Dame. Unidentified bodies were laid out there behind glass so that the public could view them and name them.
quote: the corpse was conveyed to the morgue

text: The court clerk’s office (the greffe), where evidence was stored.
quote: were deposited at the registry

text: A member of the Chamber of Peers, the upper house of parliament. Under King Louis-Philippe the king appointed peers for life.
quote: Count of Morcerf, peer of France

text: Travellers had their passports stamped by the authorities along the route. Beauchamp’s stamps run from the republic of Geneva, through the Austrian-ruled kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia, to the Ottoman Empire.
quote: examine the visa

text: Travellers arriving from Ottoman lands were held in isolation for some days for fear of plague.
quote: four days of quarantine

text: A colossal bribe. The crown (écu) was an old silver coin worth three to six francs, so this means many millions of francs.
quote: surrendered the castle for two million crowns

text: The half-century of upheaval since 1789: the Revolution, the Empire, the Restoration and the July Revolution of 1830. Beauchamp suggests few men came through it with clean hands.
quote: this revolutionary period

text: A light, sporty open carriage, usually driven by its owner.
quote: in the phaeton

text: Latin: ‘to the unknown god’. St Paul found an altar with this inscription in Athens (Acts 17:23). Albert will thank a benefactor he cannot name.
quote: I will erect an altar

text: Pontius Pilate washed his hands in front of the crowd to disclaim responsibility for Jesus’s death (Matthew 27:24).
quote: like Pilate—washing my hands

text: Italian: opera and theatre managers. The Teatro Valle is a historic theatre in Rome.
quote: the director of the Valle Theatre

text: A long covered travelling carriage of Central European origin, with room to stretch out and sleep.
quote: a good travelling britzka

text: Picturesque islands in Lake Maggiore in northern Italy, a classic tourist destination. Beauchamp names them to cover where he has really been.
quote: the Borromean Islands

text: King Francis I of France is said to have scratched ‘Souvent femme varie’ (‘woman often changes’) on a window at Chambord.
quote: Woman is fickle.

text: Travellers hired fresh horses at post stations every few leagues and paid the postilions who rode them. By keeping relays of his own horses, the count avoids the slow public system.
quote: your post-horses going at the rate of two leagues an hour

text: France was slow to build railways. By the late 1830s it had only a few short lines, far behind Britain.
quote: surpass the railway, which would not be very difficult in France

text: Heraldic terms: or is gold, azure is blue, gules is red. A charge ‘in chief’ sits in the top band of the shield.
quote: a mountain _or_, on a sea _azure_

text: From the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:5), where God visits ‘the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation’.
quote: to the third and fourth generation

text: Under King Louis-Philippe the press was split between ‘ministerial’ papers that backed the government and opposition papers like Beauchamp’s.
quote: one that was well known as a government paper

text: A dull but hot political question of the 1830s. French beet sugar competed with colonial cane sugar, and its taxation was fiercely debated.
quote: a leading article in the same paper on beet-sugar

text: The raised platform from which members address a French legislative chamber.
quote: ascended the tribune

text: Napoleon’s expedition to Egypt (1798–1801). Its soldiers and scholars brought back a knowledge of Arabic.
quote: the famous Egyptian campaign

text: The ‘Sublime Porte’: the Ottoman government, named after the gate of the grand vizier’s offices in Constantinople.
quote: his infamous bargain with the Porte

text: The Islamic calendar counts its years from the Hegira, Muhammad’s move to Medina in AD 622. The year 1247 ran from mid-1831 to mid-1832.
quote: in the year 1247 of the Hegira

text: The senior Orthodox bishop of the region, here certifying a baptism.
quote: the grand primate of Macedonia and Epirus

text: In the Aeneid, Venus gives herself away as a goddess by the way she walks: ‘vera incessu patuit dea’.
quote: which Virgil attributes to his goddesses

text: The Chamber of Peers met in the Luxembourg Palace, which has an entrance on this Left Bank street.
quote: opening into the Rue de Vaugirard

text: Since the Bible, Babylon has been a byword for a vast, worldly, pleasure-seeking city.
quote: this great Babylon of excitement

text: French: a mild oath, roughly ‘By Jove!’. It is a softened form of ‘par Dieu’ (‘by God’), like ‘pardieu’.
Throwing a glove at a man, or in his face, was the classic gesture of challenge and a mortal insult. By taking the glove, the count accepts the challenge.
quote: I consider your glove thrown

text: By duelling convention, the insulted party chose the weapons. The count gives up that right.
quote: I leave him the choice of arms

text: A large wood on the eastern edge of Paris and a favourite place for duels.
quote: in the Bois de Vincennes

text: Brooding, mysterious heroes of Romantic fiction. Lara and Manfred come from Byron’s poems, and Lord Ruthven is the aristocratic vampire of Polidori’s The Vampyre (1819).
quote: a Lara, a Manfred, a Lord Ruthven

text: Gilbert Duprez was the star tenor of the Paris Opera. From 1837 he was famous for the ringing high C he sang at full voice in Rossini’s William Tell.
quote: listen how adorably Duprez is singing

text: Rossini’s 1829 grand opera about the Swiss hero. In it the young Arnold sings ‘O Mathilde, idole de mon âme’ (‘O Mathilde, idol of my soul’) to the princess he loves.
quote: O Mathilde! idole de mon âme!

text: At the Opera, men sat in the stalls (the ‘orchestra’) or the pit, while society rented boxes. A box between the columns was one of the most prominent in the house.
quote: the box between the columns

text: French: ‘Follow me!’. It is Arnold’s rousing call to arms in William Tell, the aria where Duprez sang his famous high C.
A theatre box at the level of the stalls (the parquet), close to the stage.
quote: concealed in a parquet box

text: The waterside tavern in Marseilles, from the book’s opening chapters, where the betrothal feast was held.
quote: under the arbor of La Réserve

text: Royalists called Napoleon ‘the usurper’ because they held that he had seized a throne belonging to the Bourbons.
quote: a letter from Murat to the usurper

text: Someone who serves for pay: a hired servant or mercenary.
quote: a stipendiary of Ali

text: Gujarat in India was famed for pearls and gems. Ophir is the land in the Bible from which Solomon’s ships brought gold.
quote: the richest pearls of Guzerat and Ophir

text: Twenty million francs: a staggering fortune, at a time when a family could live decently on 2,000–3,000 francs a year.
quote: the sum of twenty millions

term: It is good to think of death
text: An echo of Ecclesiastes 7 (‘it is better to go to the house of mourning’) and the old maxim memento mori: ‘remember that you must die’.
quote: It is good to think of death.

text: A celebrated café and ice-cream parlour on the Boulevard des Italiens, a haunt of fashionable young men.
quote: I went to Tortoni’s

text: A pistol duel was thought to depend more on luck than a sword fight did. Seconds bargained over the weapons, the distance, and who would fire first.
quote: the pistol is blind

text: In Plutarch and in Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar, a ghost (Caesar’s, in Shakespeare) appears to Brutus before the battle of Philippi in 42 BC, where Brutus dies.
quote: Brutus the night before the battle of Philippi

text: A man facing pistols wore dark clothes buttoned to the chin so as not to offer a bright target. Albert’s open coat and white waistcoat look recklessly careless.
quote: painted a spot upon his heart

text: A duel abandoned on the ground. Society tended to read it as cowardice, so the man who backed down could expect sneers, fresh challenges, or both.
quote: nothing induces serious duels so much as a duel forsworn

text: Fashionable French sculptors of the day. Antoine-Louis Barye was especially admired for his small animal bronzes.
quote: bronzes by Feuchères or Barye

text: A modest street on the Left Bank of Paris, a world away from the Morcerf mansion.
quote: a small furnished house to let in the Rue des Saints-Pères

text: 3,000 francs. That was a young sailor’s hard-won savings and enough to start a modest household, but a pittance beside the count’s millions.
quote: a hundred and fifty louis

text: A tree-lined avenue in Marseilles, where the Dantès family’s little house stood.
quote: on the Allées de Meilhan

text: Widowed or ruined women of good family often withdrew to a convent, as a nun or as a paying resident. A nun was usually expected to bring a dowry.
quote: I shall take with me to some convent

text: One of the toll gates in the wall around Paris, on the road in from Vincennes.
quote: At the Barrière du Trône

text: Today’s Place des Vosges, an elegant 17th-century square in the Marais district.
quote: at the end of the Place Royale

text: Napoleon’s final defeat, on 18 June 1815, which ended the Hundred Days.
quote: deserted on the eve of the battle of Waterloo

text: In 1823 France invaded Spain to restore King Ferdinand VII’s absolute power against the Spanish liberals.
quote: guide and spy to the French army in Spain

text: A coach for hire, the taxi of the day. It was humble transport to find in a nobleman’s courtyard.
quote: a hackney-coach was standing in the middle of the yard

text: A cure-all remedy.
quote: Grandpapa says it is a panacea.

text: A prince outranks a count. Danglars, a self-styled ‘popular banker’, finds the grander title more useful.
quote: Danglars kept up the title of prince.

text: A wealthy French wedding was preceded by the signing of the marriage contract, which fixed the dowry and property arrangements, at a grand evening reception.
quote: a grand feast, a betrothal festival

text: The destroying angel who struck down the firstborn of Egypt (Exodus 12).
quote: some exterminating angel

text: The secret ‘Vehmic courts’ of medieval Westphalia, which judged offenders in secret and had them executed.
quote: there is no longer a Vehmgericht

text: Laurence Sterne (1713–68), the English author of Tristram Shandy and A Sentimental Journey.
quote: as Sterne said

text: The cursed family of Atreus in Greek myth, the line of Agamemnon and Orestes. For generations its members murdered one another.
quote: like the house of the Atreidae

text: France began conquering Algeria in 1830, and the fighting dragged on for years. Maximilian served there as a cavalry officer.
quote: the murderous nights of Algeria

term: putting the dots on the i
text: A French idiom, ‘mettre les points sur les i’: to spell something out exactly.
From the French hôtel: a grand private town house, not an inn.
quote: the house adjoining the hotel of M. de Villefort

text: The standard French lease, which the tenant could end at each three-year mark.
quote: for three, six, or nine years

text: ‘Nothing too much’ was a Greek maxim carved at Delphi. ‘I carry all my goods with me’ is credited to the sage Bias, who fled his city with nothing. Phaedrus was a Roman writer of fables.
quote: one is, I believe, from Phædrus, and the other from Bias

text: Paris boulevard theatres famous for melodrama, full of tyrannical stage fathers.
quote: the fathers of the Porte Saint-Martin and Gaîté

text: Under the Napoleonic Code, a fixed share of a parent’s estate had to go to the children. A marriage was not valid without the bride’s own consent.
quote: the provident law has deprived you of the power to disinherit me

text: Giuditta Pasta, Maria Malibran and Giulia Grisi were the great opera sopranos of the day, and they commanded enormous fees.
quote: like Pasta, Malibran, Grisi

text: John Law’s Mississippi Company (1716–20) set off a frenzy of speculation in Paris, then collapsed and ruined thousands.
quote: the fantastic Mississippi scheme

text: The French state granted private companies concessions to build and run railway lines. In the 1840s this set off a speculative boom.
quote: obtained a grant of a railway

text: Treasury bills: government IOUs, as good as cash.
quote: two drafts on the treasury

text: In France the legally binding marriage is the civil ceremony at the town hall (mairie). The church wedding follows it.
quote: on returning from the mayor’s

text: Desdemona’s father curses her for marrying against his wishes, in Shakespeare’s Othello and in Rossini’s opera Otello, which Paris loved.
quote: Brabantio’s malediction on Desdemona

text: Eugénie’s pocket money alone, 12,000 francs a year, is many times a skilled worker’s annual wage.
quote: the thousand francs I give you monthly

text: Molière’s characters, played at the Théâtre-Français (the Comédie-Française). Dorante and Valère are stock names for smooth young gentlemen, and Alceste is the blunt hero of The Misanthrope.
quote: Dorante or Valère reply to Alceste

text: A harem. The count is sending Andrea up with mock ‘Eastern scruples’.
quote: I, who have a seraglio at Cairo

text: At a society wedding, the notaries read the marriage contract aloud at a reception. The two families, then distinguished guests, added their signatures as an honour.
quote: the signature of the contract

text: A member of the Académie française, the official guardian of the French language. The narrator uses the word for a maker of elegant phrases.
quote: An Academician would say

text: The beautiful shepherd of Greek myth, cast into an endless sleep and loved by the Moon. He was a favourite subject for ornate clocks.
quote: representing Endymion asleep

text: Nicolas Boileau, the 17th-century poet and critic who laid down the rules of French classical taste.
quote: what Boileau calls

text: Latin: ‘seeking whom he may devour’. The phrase comes from 1 Peter 5:8, where the devil prowls ‘as a roaring lion’.
A police commissary on official duty wore a tricolour sash as his badge of office.
quote: girded with his scarf

text: Cholera swept Paris in 1832 and killed some 18,000 people. It remained a byword for sudden terror and flight.
quote: a case of plague or of cholera morbus

text: Foreign government bonds traded on the Paris Bourse. Spanish bonds swung wildly with Spain’s civil war, and Haiti’s 1825 loan, raised to pay France an indemnity for recognition, was notoriously shaky.
quote: the rise and fall of Spanish funds, of Haitian bonds

text: Travel, even inside France, required a passport describing the bearer, and post-houses would not supply horses without one.
quote: M. Léon d’Armilly, twenty years of age

text: In Greek myth the hero Hercules served Queen Omphale as a slave, and the two swapped clothes and roles.
quote: I was Hercules, and you only the pale Omphale

text: The warrior women of Greek legend.
quote: You are a perfect Amazon

text: Bold women of the Bible. Judith beheaded the enemy general Holofernes, and Delilah overcame Samson by cutting his hair.
quote: as strong as a Judith or a Delilah

text: 400 francs: a large bribe for a laundress, perhaps half a year’s earnings.
quote: she had been promised twenty louis

text: The man who rides one of the horses of a post-chaise to drive it.
quote: said the postilion

text: A toll gate in the wall around Paris, on the road north. Just beyond it lay the village of La Villette.
quote: the Barrière Saint-Martin

text: The trousseau is the bride’s own linen and clothes. The corbeille (‘basket’) holds the bridegroom’s gifts to her of jewels, lace and shawls, which were put on display for the guests.
Fine, costly bobbin lace from Valenciennes in northern France. Shawls of Indian cashmere were equally prized luxury gifts.
quote: cashmere shawls, Valenciennes lace

text: A village on the main road north from Paris towards Senlis and Flanders, not the museum.
quote: Towards the Louvres.

text: The administrative department just north of Paris, around Senlis and Compiègne.
quote: the department of the Oise

text: A town about 80 km north of Paris, with a royal palace and a great forest.
quote: Compiègne, that royal residence and fortified town

text: In Greek myth Achilles was hidden on Scyros, disguised as a girl among the king’s daughters, and there he loved the princess Deidamia.
quote: which represented Achilles with Deidamia

text: In the gendarmerie, France’s rural military police, a brigadier is a corporal commanding a small post, not a general.
quote: who was a brigadier

text: The Court of Assizes, where serious crimes were tried before a jury.
quote: an arrest meant the assizes

text: The wish that all Rome had a single neck is usually credited to Caligula, not Nero (Suetonius, Life of Caligula).
quote: made Nero wish that the Roman world

text: The old prison inside the Palais de Justice in Paris, where prisoners were held before trial.
quote: incarcerated in the Conciergerie
